paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A triple junction is the point at which the boundaries of three tectonic plates come together. Each of the three boundaries is one of three types: a ridge (R), a trench (T) or a transform fault (F). Triple junctions can be described by the kinds of plate margin meeting there. Fault–fault–trench is shortened to F-F-T, and ridge–ridge–ridge to R-R-R.

paragraphs.heading: Ridges and trenches
paragraphs.text: In this scheme, a ridge is a structure that produces lithosphere symmetrically, at right angles to the relative velocity of the plates on its two sides, though this does not always apply. A trench is a structure that consumes lithosphere from one side only.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea began
paragraphs.text: The term was traditionally used for the meeting of three divergent boundaries, or spreading ridges. Ideally these three meet at angles near 120°. In plate tectonics theory, when a continent breaks up, three divergent boundaries form and radiate from a central point, which is the triple junction. One of them fails, and the other two keep spreading to form an ocean. The term has since come to mean any point where three tectonic plates meet.

paragraphs.heading: The South Atlantic example
paragraphs.text: The south Atlantic Ocean began to open at the south of South America and Africa. The opening reached a triple junction in what is now the Gulf of Guinea, and from there it continued to the west. The Benue Trough, which trends north-east, is the failed arm of this junction.

paragraphs.heading: Stable and unstable
paragraphs.text: A stable junction is one that keeps its geometry over time as the plates involved move. Only a few of the possible types of triple junction are stable through time. An unstable junction changes with time. It may become another form of triple junction, as RRF junctions easily evolve into FFR junctions, or change geometry, or simply not be feasible, as with FFF junctions. An FFF junction is inherently unstable, and this instability is believed to have caused the Pacific plate to form about 190 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Why a flat drawing is enough
paragraphs.text: Triple junctions are easiest to understand by treating the plates as rigid pieces that move over Earth's surface. Then nothing needs to be known about the inside of the Earth or the geological details of its crust. On a sphere, the motions of plates are described as relative rotations about what are called Euler poles. The area around a triple junction is small compared with the sphere, and it is usually far enough from the pole of rotation, so the relative motion across a boundary can be treated as constant along that boundary. The analysis can therefore usually be carried out on a flat surface, with vectors defining the motions.

paragraphs.heading: Why three faults cannot last
paragraphs.text: Stability can be tested with a drawing. The relative velocities of the three plates make a triangle whose side lengths are proportional to those velocities. One line is drawn for each boundary, and the junction can exist stably only if the three lines are able to meet at a single point. For a transform fault, the line must lie along the matching side of the triangle. Three lines that lie along the sides of a triangle can meet at one point only when the sides have zero length, which corresponds to zero relative motion between the plates. Faults are required to be active for this assessment, so an FFF junction can never be stable.
